665833_hitter.text: Oneil Cruz is one of the most violent contact-makers in baseball — 96.0 mph average exit velocity and 59.2% hard-hit rate both sit at the 100th percentile — but he gives a huge chunk of it back at the plate because he simply can't make consistent contact, whiffing at 37.8% (2nd percentile) with a 34.6% K% that ranks dead last. The ValuCast projection of .230 AVG / .407 SLG reflects that gap: 20 home runs in 530 PA is realistic given the power floor, but the strikeouts and low contact rate will keep him from reaching his xwOBA ceiling of .315. Medium confidence reflects the volatility between his elite tooling and his severe swing-and-miss issue.

700933_pitcher.text: Chris Cortez is a right-handed pitcher generating swing-and-miss stuff (11.7 K/9 across 15.3 IP at AA) but fighting serious command issues that have inflated his ERA to 4.7 with a 1.96 WHIP. His 8.8 BB/9 is the primary constraint—translated to the MLB equivalent, that projects to 7.2 BB/9, well above league average and a structural ceiling on his value. This is a thin sample at an early stage, so the command profile may sharpen with additional reps, but right now he profiles as a depth arm or bullpen option rather than a starting path.

701056_pitcher.text: Josh Grosz is a bat-missing righthander running elite strikeout rates at AA—13.2 K/9 (92nd percentile)—but his walk rate of 5.1 BB/9 and 1.37 WHIP signal he hasn't yet earned command consistency at the upper minors. The MLB-equivalent translation projects a 4.1 BB/9 and 9.4 K/9, meaningful improvements but still above-average risk on the control axis. With only 30 innings in this sample, confidence is low; the strikeout profile is real, but the command floor remains unproven.

701178_pitcher.text: Rafe Schlesinger is a left-hander generating swing-and-miss at a high rate—89th percentile K/9 at 12.0 K/9 (minor-league line)—but control has deteriorated sharply in his AA debut, posting an 8.64 ERA over just 8.3 innings with a 3.2 BB/9. His A+ sample of 45 IP shows the profile more clearly: 12.6 K/9 with better command (3.6 BB/9) and a 22.2% K-BB%, but a 1.51 WHIP and 4.4 ERA suggest the strikeouts haven't translated to dominance. The immediate risk is real control trouble at the new level; the current sample is too thin to confirm whether this is early-season noise or a meaningful step-down in execution.

701327_hitter.text: Elijah Green is a high-strikeout prospect who shows enough power to project as a reserve but struggles sharply with contact—45.5% K% in A+ play ranks in the 1st percentile against the ValuCast hitter pool. His .172 ISO (65th percentile) and 10.9% BB% suggest he can hit for some damage when he connects, but a .204 AVG and .292 OBP across 257 plate appearances demonstrate he is not connecting enough to stay playable at present rates. The translation to MLB equivalents projects 41.6% K% and .131 ISO, well below average, which compounds the contact problem—this is a swing-and-miss profile without the power floor to absorb the whiffs. With the sample current and live, confidence in the overall arc depends on whether Green can demonstrate material improvement in contact rates; right now the risk is skewed heavily toward continued strikeout dominance over value creation.

701328_pitcher.text: Jackson Ferris pitches from the left side but has shown significantly elevated walk rates paired with below-average strikeout production in his AAA exposure—a 5.7 BB/9 and 7.3 K/9 that grade in the 11th-29th percentiles of the pitcher pool. His MLB-equivalent translation projects a 4.4 BB/9 with 7.6 K/9, still well behind league average and suggesting command and stuff both remain developmental concerns. The primary risk is control; even with the AAA-to-MLB walk-rate adjustment, the K-BB% gap (8.9% vs 13.5% MLB average) indicates limited margin for error as a starter. At 22 with just 39.7 innings at the upper level, this sample is too thin to anchor a confident read.

701337_hitter.text: Ethan Petry is a power-first hitter showing elite-percentile ISO and OPS against AA competition but struggling badly with plate discipline in his brief exposure at that level. Over 37 PA at AA, he's struck out at 37.8% while walking just 5.4%, and his .206 AVG reflects contact failure rather than a power problem—the 22-year-old's .500 SLG suggests he's still barreling the ball when he makes contact. His A+ track record (.297/.392/.521 over 194 PA, 86th percentile ISO) shows a more functional approach, but the current strikeout rate and BB% collapse signal he's not yet ready to exploit his power at AA. This is a thin sample in real time, so the read leans on how sharply his discipline has degraded on the promotion.

701339_hitter.text: Marek Houston is a contact-first shortstop who is making consistent hard contact at A+ while showing advanced pitch recognition for his age. His .325 AVG and .406 OBP sit at the 98th and 91st percentiles respectively in the ValuCast pool, built on 11.9% BB% discipline paired with just 18.3% K%. The ISO of .136 lags well behind league average and his percentile rank—he's a singles hitter who will need to develop more thump to profile as more than a utility bat at the next level. The 268-PA sample is live and current, though his upside remains capped by modest raw power metrics.

701364_pitcher.text: Jamie Arnold is a 22-year-old lefty at AA who gets through innings without dominating them — 9.8 K/9 in the minors translates to a below-average 8.3 at the MLB level against a league mean of 8.6, and his 4.4 BB/9 translates to 4.4 up top against a league mean of 3.2, which is the real problem. The WHIP sitting at the 27th percentile in his AA pitcher pool tells you the walk rate isn't hiding; it's showing up in baserunners, and until the command tightens, the back-end starter projection stays a projection. ValuCast has him cooling — down 5.4 in the last three days — and that aligns with a profile where the floor (depth arm) is doing most of the probability work, with 34% of outcomes landing in depth/relief against 19% as a rotation piece.

701388_pitcher.text: Cijntje is a strikeout arm with a walk problem — that tension is the whole story. At AA in 2026, he's fanning batters at 10.9 K/9 (translates to 8.8 at the MLB level, right at league average), but the 4.7 BB/9 is bleeding him dry: his MLB-equivalent K-BB% of 12.1% sits below the big-league average of 13.5%, and the 5.70 ERA reflects what happens when you give hitters free passes at this rate. The projection sees a multi-inning or setup reliever as the ceiling, with 64% of outcomes landing as a useful MLB arm — and moving him to shorter stints could let the swing-and-miss play up while the command issues matter less. He's cooled in ValuCast rankings, down 6.0 points in the last three days, and until that BB/9 moves, this is a talent that needs a role change more than more time in a rotation.

701394_hitter.text: Ehrhard is a patient, on-base-first center fielder who has quietly put together one of the cleaner AAA bat profiles in the system. His .386 OBP and 14% walk rate in 345 PA this season translate to an 11.4% MLB-equivalent walk rate against an 8.5% league average — the approach is real, not a PCL mirage. The raw line (.281/.386/.472, 12 home runs, 9 steals) checks out across the board, with his MLB-equivalent ISO landing right at the league average .152, which puts a ceiling on the "power bat" framing but keeps him as a genuine offensive contributor. ValuCast has him rising — up +0.42 score points and climbing eight spots in three days — and the projection pegs a low-end everyday regular ceiling, with the approach being the one tool that gives him a real shot to stick.

701398_hitter.text: Sal Stewart is a 22-year-old power bat who makes genuine loud contact — a 15.4% barrel rate puts him in the 92nd percentile, and the .483 xSLG (85th percentile) confirms he earns his thump rather than borrowing it from a friendly park. The disconnect between that xSLG and a 28.1% whiff rate (32nd percentile) is the real tension in his profile: he can do real damage when he connects, but he gives away too many at-bats chasing spin he can't handle yet. The 11.5% walk rate (75th percentile) says the zone awareness is developing, which is encouraging at 22, and ValuCast's current projection of 29 HR, 100 RBI, and 18 SB across 684 PA reflects a player who could grow into a genuine middle-of-the-order corner bat if that whiff rate comes down even a few ticks.

701480_pitcher.text: Bryce Cunningham is a right-handed depth arm prospect whose current profile is dragged down by modest strikeout stuff—9.4 K/9 (46th percentile) and a 12.7% K-BB% (51st percentile)—paired with a command problem that translates to a 4.2 BB/9 at the MLB level. His WHIP of 1.23 sits at the 81st percentile, suggesting he avoids hard contact or damage, but the walk rate is the central risk: he's allowing free passes at a rate well above league average (3.2 BB/9), which will cost him in any serious MLB role. ValuCast ranks him rising, and the projection sees upside over two to three years, but with only 37 innings banked, confidence here is legitimately low—the sample is fresh but too thin to anchor much certainty.

701481_hitter.text: Ryan Campos is a left-handed hitter building a compelling on-base profile through disciplined approach, not just raw power—his .409 OBP and 15.7% BB% rank in the 83rd–93rd percentiles despite a 21.5% K% that leaves room to improve contact. The .881 OPS and .183 ISO on 242 PA at AA show a hitter who reaches base consistently and drives the ball enough to project as a bench or platoon bat with medium risk over the next one to two years. His floor is reserve depth; the main constraint is modest raw power and a strikeout rate that will need to stay controlled to maintain value at the MLB level. This is a fresh, moderate-confidence sample from active AA play.

701527_hitter.text: Mike Sirota is a 23-year-old center fielder showing elite plate discipline paired with surprising power, operating at a .480 OBP with a .516 slugging line over 123 PA at AA. His 22% walk rate (99th percentile) and 22% strikeout rate sit in productive balance, though the strikeout floor and modest power translate to only .161 ISO at the MLB level. The near-term ceiling is a useful bench or platoon bat; sample size is fresh but still thin, and secondary tools remain unproven in the data.

701538_hitter.text: Jackson Merrill is a plus athlete with a contact problem. The hard-hit profile is real — 46.6% Hard-Hit and a 9.8% Barrel rate are legitimate — but a 35.1% Chase and 28.0% Whiff rate are bleeding the life out of it, which is exactly why his xwOBA sits at .303 (29th percentile) despite the raw thump. He's fast enough (28.9 ft/s sprint speed, 89th percentile) to squeeze value out of a 26-steal season, but the ValuCast projection of .230/.289/.385 at 660 PA reflects a guy whose chase habits keep him from being the hitter the exit velo suggests he could be. Until the zone decisions tighten, the speed and power are tax deductions, not dividends.

701542_pitcher.text: Will Warren is a back-of-the-rotation starter who lives by limiting walks and spinning the ball — not by blowing hitters away. His 7.5% BB% puts him in the 66th percentile, and that control is the thing keeping his xERA at 4.04 and his xwOBA at .312, both sitting right at league average. The story underneath is a real tension: his 2540 rpm fastball spin is elite (92nd percentile), yet his Whiff% (22.9%) and Chase% (28.8%) land in the low-to-mid 30s, meaning he hasn't converted that spin into swing-and-miss at a rate that would push him past a no. 4 profile. ValuCast projects 159 innings with a 3.87 ERA, which is a touch friendlier than his xERA suggests — the command edge earns some of that gap, but he'll need to get more out of that spin to stay in the rotation long-term.

701590_pitcher.text: Khal Stephen is a 23-year-old right-hander whose value lives in the run prevention column, not the strikeout ledger — and that gap is what defines him. At AA this season, his 3.40 ERA and 1.40 WHIP are real production over 55 innings, but the 8.0 K/9 translates to just 7.5 at the MLB level against a league average of 8.6, and his K-BB% of 11% sits in the 39th percentile of his pitcher pool — he's keeping runs off the board without missing bats, which is a fragile formula as he climbs. The command is passable (3.8 BB/9, 67th percentile), but until the strikeout rate gives him a second lever to pull, the projection points toward a multi-inning or setup role rather than a rotation spot — ValuCast sees a 68% chance he becomes a useful MLB arm with a depth floor, and he's risen four spots in the last three days.

701616_hitter.text: Caleb Lomavita is a 23-year-old catcher whose bat plays through raw power — 11 home runs in 217 AA plate appearances, a .263 ISO that translates to roughly .176 at the MLB level against a league average of .150. The contact and OBP picture is messier: a .242/.327/.505 AA line (combined 2026) with a .257 BABIP suggests he's not getting lucky to prop that average up, he's just not making enough contact, and the walk rate doesn't cover it — his OBP sits at the 31st percentile against AA peers even as his ISO checks 94th. The projection sees a bench or platoon outcome as the most likely path, with the power as the one trait that keeps a regular ceiling in the conversation. ValuCast has him moving up +1.0 in the last three days in rankings.

701649_hitter.text: James Triantos makes contact at an elite rate — his 14% strikeout rate at AAA translates to a projected 17.5% at the MLB level, well below the 22.0% league average, and that's the engine here. The hit tool grades as the carrying skill, but the approach is the ceiling wall: a 4% walk rate in 316 PA this season at AAA translates to just 5.8% at the MLB level against an 8.5% average, which means he's squeezed between a real bat and no on-base margin for error. ValuCast projects him as a bench or platoon bat, with 84% probability at that role and only 5% odds at becoming a regular — the projection sees more upside than today's value suggests, but that's conditioned on the walk rate growing. He's moved up +11 spots in ValuCast's rankings over the last three days, a sign the contact is getting attention, but the approach is the thing he has to fix.

701656_pitcher.text: Logan Henderson has flashed mid-rotation upside in early AAA action, posting a 1.02 ERA with 13.2 K/9 and a 23.3% K-BB% over 17.7 innings. Control remains a concern—his 4.6 BB/9 translates to 3.6 MLB BB/9, above league average—and the injury status (currently on the injured reserve) clouds near-term availability. This is a thin, live sample from a young right-hander with ceiling; confidence is limited until he logs meaningful healthy innings at this level.

701679_pitcher.text: Brody Brecht is a high-strikeout arm still hunting for command; 13.5 K/9 ranks 94th percentile in the ValuCast pitcher pool, but a 6.5 BB/9 and 1.4 WHIP reflect a starter who is not yet locating consistently enough to grade as reliable. The K-BB% of 17.8% sits at 77th percentile, which shows upside, but the 5.23 ERA translates to a walk rate the system projects as MLB-average or slightly worse (4.6 BB/9 equivalent). This is a depth profile with significant development risk—only 20.7 innings in the current sample, and low confidence in the translation given thin workload.

701680_pitcher.text: RJ Sales is a right-handed depth arm still assembling the stuff to miss bats consistently—he struck out 9.5 per 9 in 94.7 IP at A-ball last season, but that translates to just 7.1 K/9 at the MLB level, well below league average. Command grades as a relative strength (2.7 BB/9, 90th percentile), though control doesn't overcome insufficient strikeout ability. The core risk is modest miss and run prevention (ERA 2.85 in a thin, prior-season sample from June), leaving him ceiling'd as organizational depth rather than a rotation contributor over the next two to three years. ValuCast is rising on him (+14.6 points in three days), but the sample is stale and the strikeout profile remains the primary constraint.

701717_pitcher.text: Dalton Pence is a left-handed pitcher showing elite command and contact management in short-season AA action, evidenced by a 2.56 ERA (91st percentile) and 1.04 WHIP (94th percentile) across 31.7 IP. His 8.2 K/9 and 2.8 BB/9 sit at the 24th and 88th percentiles respectively, indicating strong control but modest strikeout production for a prospect profile. The primary risk is insufficient swing-and-miss; his MLB translation of 8.0 K/9 is below-average MLB rate, which limits ceiling if fastball velocity or secondary pitches don't develop further. Small active sample warrants patience before projecting sustained depth-role utility.

701750_hitter.text: Bennett Thompson is a high-contact, high-walk hitter running a 99th-percentile approach at A+, getting on base at elite rates (.495 OBP) with surprising pop (.536 SLG, .222 ISO). His 25.7% walk rate and 17.1% strikeout rate anchor a disciplined profile that translates to a projected 14.9% BB% and 21.7% K% in MLB context. The main risk is that power plays down sharply in translation—from .222 ISO to .150 MLB-equivalent—and catcher depth of role limits ceiling, leaving this as a bench or platoon outcome even if the bat stays intact. The 210 PA sample is current and clean, but early in the season.

701762_hitter.text: Nick Kurtz is a walking, mashing first baseman who beats you with power and patience before contact even enters the conversation. His 94.3 mph average exit velocity, 18.7% barrel rate, and 58.5% hard-hit rate are all sitting at the 98th percentile — the ball simply sounds different off his bat — and a 19.3% walk rate that is literally off the percentile chart tells you pitchers already know it. The one real tension in his profile is the 36.2% whiff rate (4th percentile), which explains why the xBA (.257) lags so far behind the xwOBA (.390); the power and discipline are elite, but if he's going to sustain a .271 AVG as ValuCast's projection calls for, contact quality will need to outpace contact frequency. The projection — .271/.403/.519, 37 home runs — treats him as a frontline offensive first baseman, and the underlying Statcast profile at 23 years old gives you every reason to believe the ceiling is real.

701771_hitter.text: Billy Amick is swinging for the fences but missing too much to generate consistent contact at Double-A. His .259 ISO ranks in the 95th percentile of the minor-league pool, but he's striking out in 30.8% of his plate appearances (20th percentile) while batting just .198 over 279 PA, leaving his .323 OBP and .78 OPS well below average for the level. The hit tool is the blocker here—until he cuts the strikeout rate or finds more barrels in the zone, the power upside stays capped. ValuCast projects him as organizational depth with 85% probability of a bench role, and the current 279-PA sample is fresh and clear.

701778_hitter.text: Jace Avina is a high-leverage power hitter who will strike out often and accept a low walk rate—a bet on impact over contact. His .287 ISO and .941 OPS (98th and 97th percentiles respectively) show raw thump, but a 29.8% K rate paired with just 10.2% BB rate signals an aggressive, all-or-nothing approach that has limited his hit tool to average (55-grade hit against high whiff). The main risk is whether that strikeout rate will play in the majors; when translated to MLB equivalent, it projects to 28.8% K%, well above league average. ValuCast's projection—bench or platoon role with 85% probability—reflects a skill shape built on power and impact, but the current sample of 245 PA is still emerging.

701780_pitcher.text: Tanner McDougal is a right-handed starter showing promising strike-to-walk ratios—a 3.75 K-BB% on 10.1 K/9 and 4.9 BB/9 at AAA—but he's working through just 24 innings, making any durability or consistency read speculative at best. The ERA (3.00) and WHIP (1.04) rank well percentile-wise, yet control volatility (walk rate at 44th percentile) and the thin, current workload create real noise in the signal. Given the 24-inning sample size and low confidence in translation, treat this as a depth prospect with significant remain-to-be-proven markers rather than a settled performer.

701785_hitter.text: Kaelen Culpepper is a 23-year-old shortstop doing real damage at AAA — not just surviving the level, but posting a .492 SLG and .220 ISO across 295 PA with 15 stolen bases layered on top. The translation softens it some, but a projected 10.3% walk rate against a 20.0% strikeout rate still beats MLB averages in both directions, and that's the bat shape you want: a guy who takes a pitch, hits for power, and doesn't give at-bats away. The projection sees everyday upside with more ceiling ahead than the current line already shows, though ValuCast has him slipping four spots over the last three days — worth watching but not a reason to move off him yet.

701795_pitcher.text: Drew Beam operates as a high-walk starter with below-average command, posting a 3.5 BB/9 and 6.9 K/9 across 61.3 innings at Double-A. The core problem is efficiency: his 6.02 ERA and 1.39 WHIP reflect a pitcher who cannot keep hitters off the bases and lacks the strikeout rate to compensate, sitting at just the 7th percentile in K/9. The walk rate (75th percentile) is his lone strength, but it's insufficient to offset weak strikeout stuff and a 26th-percentile ERA profile; confidence here is moderate given only two months of active sample.

701852_hitter.text: Drew Cavanaugh is a left-handed hitter who is manufacturing loud contact at AAA—.571 SLG with .241 ISO in 137 plate appearances—despite hitting only .330 in a strikeout-prone profile (24.8% K%). The 99th-percentile OBP (.445) and 99th-percentile AVG mask a fundamental swing-and-miss problem: his K% sits at the 50th percentile even as he makes the ball travel at an elite rate, and his approach grades only as average (55 on BB% / BB-K%). His ceiling projects as a bench or platoon piece, with an 85% probability of that role; the floor is reserve depth. The sample is live and substantial, though he's just 137 PA into the season and moving up in ValuCast's rankings.

701906_hitter.text: Trevor Cohen is a contact-oriented left-handed hitter showing disciplined plate management — he's hitting .295 with a 12.4% walk rate against just 14.0% strikeouts at A+. His 91st-percentile batting average and 82nd-percentile OBP reflect a balanced, line-drive approach, but his 43rd-percentile ISO (.137) and sub-average power production expose limited impact upside. The projection carries modest confidence: he's a bench or organizational-depth candidate with 85% probability, ceiling around two to three years out, anchored by average hit tools and near-nothing on the power side. The current sample is live and sizable, but his floor is real.

701908_pitcher.text: David Hagaman is a high-strikeout arm with serious control problems who projects as a depth-level pitcher two to three years out. He's punching out batters at an 11.3 K/9 (77th percentile) but walking 6.2 per nine (23rd percentile), yielding a K-BB% of 12.0% that sits below league average. The main risk is command—his 1.74 WHIP and 4.37 ERA on a thin 35-inning A+ sample suggest his stuff doesn't translate to consistent outs yet, and his floor is relief work. The small current sample limits confidence, but the strikeout rate is real enough to warrant continued tracking.

702056_pitcher.text: Trey Yesavage is a contact-suppressor who earns his outs through deception and movement, not overpowering stuff — his xERA sits at 3.18 and xwOBA at .279, both in the 81st percentile, while his 94.4 mph fastball and 2269 rpm spin sit right around league average. The tension in his profile is real: a 29.3% whiff rate (78th percentile) without a chase rate that backs it up means hitters are swinging and missing at pitches in the zone, which is genuinely useful, but his 10.9% walk rate (22nd percentile) is the thing that decides whether he's a mid-rotation starter or a guy who unravels in a bad inning. ValuCast projects a 3.81 ERA over 141.1 innings, which suggests the underlying contact quality holds and the walks stay just manageable enough — at 22, with that xERA, there's real room here if he ever tightens the zone.

702253_hitter.text: Cam Collier is a 21-year-old third baseman who hits the ball hard enough to matter but not often enough yet to trust. His .179 ISO at AA is real — the power grades out at the 66th percentile among this hitter pool — but a .221/.312/.400 line over 333 PA tells you contact is still the thing standing between him and a legitimate big-league conversation. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 26.4%, above the 22.0% league average, and his walk rate essentially matches the big-league mean at 8.8%, so the approach isn't the problem; bat-to-ball is. ValuCast projects a bench/platoon outcome as the most likely landing spot, with the projection carrying more upside than today's value suggests, and he's ticked up +1.1 in ValuCast's rankings over the last three days.

702255_pitcher.text: Brandon Barriera is a left-handed starter running 7.9 K/9 against 6.3 BB/9 over his first 17 innings at A-ball, showing a strikeout rate near league average but walk rate well above it. The control problem is the defining issue—translated to MLB equivalent, his 4.5 BB/9 still sits well north of the 3.2 average—and there's no secondary skill in the sample to offset it. With only 17 innings to work from, confidence in any directional read remains low; he'll need sustained reps to prove the strikeout rate is real or whether command improves.

702261_hitter.text: Termarr Johnson is a walk machine who hasn't figured out how to turn patience into production yet. His 16% walk rate at AAA translates to a 12.2% MLB-equivalent BB% — well above the 8.5% league average — but that discipline lives in a bat currently hitting .191 with a .256 BABIP, and the MLB-equivalent strikeout rate projects to 25.6%, above average. The approach is real; the hit tool and power are not, with a .107 ISO and an OPS that sits in the 15th percentile among his peers over 287 PA. The projection sees mostly a bench or depth outcome from here, with the walk rate as the one piece worth betting on if the contact ever catches up.

702262_hitter.text: Jared Jones is a high-contact power hitter who makes hard, frequent contact at the plate, posting a .322 AVG with .525 SLG and a 97th-percentile batting average across 212 A+ plate appearances. His 15.6% BB rate is solid, and his .203 ISO ranks in the 78th percentile among the ValuCast hitter pool. The critical liability is a 30.2% strikeout rate (22nd percentile), which when translated to MLB equivalents stays near 30.1%—well above the 22% big-league average—and his power and walk rates both compress significantly in translation. The sample is current and adequate, though projection to bench or platoon utility makes sense given the strikeout floor and modest profile depth.

702264_hitter.text: Gavin Kilen is a left-handed shortstop showing disciplined contact skills—he's striking out in only the 93rd percentile while maintaining a .282/.356/.435 line across 281 PA at A+. His 14.6% K rate translates to a manageable 19.8% at the MLB level, well below league average, though his ISO of .153 projects to just .123 in the majors, suggesting limited raw power. The core risk is that power development has lagged; without it, he projects as a utility-grade regular rather than an everyday bat, even with strong bat control. The sample is fresh and sufficient, but power evolution will determine whether his hit tool can sustain value.

702266_pitcher.text: Dylan Lesko is a 22-year-old right-handed pitcher operating with fringe command and limited swing-and-miss depth relative to his prospect standing. He's struck out 10.1 per 9 innings while walking 7.2 per 9 in his current 22.3-inning A-ball sample, translating to a 5.1 BB/9 in MLB equivalents—well above the 3.2 league average. The clearest problem is his walk rate; ValuCast grades his command at 20, and even in a small sample his control has become a real drag on upside. ValuCast ranks him 228th and has cooled on him in the past three days, reflecting the volatility of early-season shallow samples and the gap between prospect pedigree and current stuff.

702270_hitter.text: Malcolm Moore is a power-first catcher with elite raw bat speed and explosive ISO (.261 in minor leagues, 92nd percentile in the current pool) but punishes himself with high strikeout rates that erode actual contact and on-base ability—his BB% is just 3.8% in his current AA stint, sitting only in the 27th percentile. The fundamental flaw is discipline: he swings and misses too often (11.5% K% in AA, climbing to 22.6% when translated to MLB context) and doesn't draw enough walks to offset it, leaving him a feast-or-famine offensive profile. At 22 with just 26 PAs at this level, the current sample is too thin to trust, but his A+ track record (.542 SLG, .387 OBP over 217 PAs) suggests he has enough bat to stick as organizational depth—if he can cut strikeouts without surrendering the power.

702271_pitcher.text: Nazier Mulé is a high-strikeout arm still learning to harness his stuff—he sits at 12.5 K/9 (87th percentile) but pairs that with a 7.2 BB/9 walk rate that trails only the 13th percentile of the pitcher pool. The core issue is command: his K-BB% of 12.9 lands exactly at the median, meaning the strikeouts aren't yet translating to competitive advantage once walks are factored in. With only 22.3 innings in the books at A+, confidence in this read is low; the sample is too thin to project role or ceiling with any certainty.

702273_pitcher.text: Noah Schultz is a high-spin starter with the strikeout stuff to miss bats at the upper minors, posting a 13.2 K/9 over his early AAA run. The command work is clean so far—3.0 BB/9 and a 30.4% K-BB%—but the primary risk is the extreme thinness of the sample: just 18.3 innings limits any firm read on how his stuff plays in extended action or against upper-level lineups. This projection carries low confidence given the sample size and needs several more weeks of sustained performance to validate the early sparkle.

702274_pitcher.text: Chase Shores is a young righthander generating premium strikeout stuff—13.5 K/9 in his A+ debut—but walking 5.7 per nine, a rate that translates to 4.1 BB/9 at the MLB level and sits above league average. The K-BB% of 20.3% looks clean in the minor leagues but projects to just 13.3% at the big-league level, suggesting the strikeouts may not carry while the control lag persists. This is a thin 17-inning sample from June 2026, so confidence in any projection remains low until he logs consecutive months of work.

The primary risk is control: a 25-grade BB/9 projection and 3.2 BB/9 in the MLB translation suggest he will leak baserunners despite the strikeouts, capping his ceiling at useful depth rather than starter potential. The current AAA sample is too thin to signal meaningful change in either direction.

805422_pitcher.text: Nate Snead is a right-handed depth pitcher showing modest control but limited carry — he sits at 5.9 K/9 (2nd percentile) and 3.0 BB/9 (85th percentile) over 21.3 IP at AA. The core problem is strikeout rate; his 7.4 K-BB% ranks in the 23rd percentile, and his translated K/9 of 7.4 against an MLB average of 8.6 leaves little margin for luck. His era and WHIP suggest he's managing outcomes reasonably well, but that run prevention cannot sustain without more miss in the zone. The sample is fresh and active, though still modest in depth.

805706_pitcher.text: AJ Russell is a strikeout machine with a command question mark attached — 14.2 K/9 and a 28% K-BB% across A/A+ this year are genuinely elite numbers for a 22-year-old right-hander, but 4.0 BB/9 is the thread that could unravel the whole thing at higher levels. The MLB-equivalent translation (low confidence, 32 IP) puts him at 9.0 K/9 versus a league average of 8.6, which is fine, but the 3.9 translated BB/9 against a 3.2 average tells you the command gap doesn't disappear when you adjust for competition. Projection has him as a useful MLB arm — most likely a depth or relief role — with the miss carrying him and the walk rate capping the ceiling; ValuCast has him cooling slightly, down three spots over the last three days.

805725_pitcher.text: Jake Miller shows control-first pitching early in his A+ stint, posting a 2.25 ERA with a 17.6 K-BB% over a thin 4 IP current sample. His MLB-equivalent translation suggests modest strikeout stuff (8.1 K/9) alongside a control profile that translates acceptably (13.2 K-BB%), though the walk rate climbs sharply in projection (2.9 BB/9 vs. 1.0 in the minor-league line). The sample is too small—only 9 IP of starter workload—to anchor confidence in either the control consistency or the depth of his role, and stale data within weeks could shift the picture quickly.

805779_hitter.text: Jacob Wilson is a light-contact, power-starved shortstop whose bat control masks a severe flywheel problem: his 1.7% barrel rate and 84.2 mph average exit velo rank in the bottom 5%, forcing him to rely on hit-tool sequencing rather than force to generate offense. The projection line of .286/.328/.410 and 10 home runs over 507 plate appearances reflects a 24-year-old who can find base hits (70th percentile xBA) but has almost no margin for error in power production and will struggle to accumulate runs in a lineup. His elite strikeout discipline (11.7% K rate, 94th percentile) and strong defensive positioning (94th percentile OAA) keep him in the field, but the offensive ceiling is genuinely shallow—a back-half utility bat in a competitive roster. Confidence is medium given the disconnect between his hit ability and power ceiling.

805790_pitcher.text: Cody Bowker is a strike-throwing right-hander building a case as a useful MLB depth arm, leaning on command and modest miss rather than dominance. His A-level track shows 14.52 K/9 and 4.54 BB/9 over 39.7 IP, placing him in the 98th percentile for strikeouts per nine and 97th for K-BB% among comparable pitchers. The hard ceiling is a mid-rotation starter—his current A+ sample of 8 IP is too thin to trust, and his MLB-equivalent translation (4.3 BB/9, 8.9 K/9 after age/level adjustment) suggests a reliever or depth starter who doesn't miss enough bats to dominate. The projection calls for two to three years; confidence is modest given only 8 innings at the new level.

805793_pitcher.text: Landen Maroudis is a young right-handed pitcher whose command has become the immediate problem—he's walking 5.1 per 9 innings (40th percentile) while generating only 7.0 K/9, leaving him with a 4.4% K-BB differential (12th percentile) over 42.7 innings at A+. His 7.17 ERA and 1.88 WHIP reflect a pitcher who is not missing enough bats and is giving up too many free passes to survive at the next level. The A+ sample is current and sufficient in volume to trust the read, though his modest strikeout rate limits upside even if command tightens.

805795_hitter.text: Aidan Miller is a patient, contact-oriented bat who hasn't yet convinced anyone he can carry a lineup spot. At AA last season, his 15% walk rate and .382 OBP over 489 PA show genuine feel for the strike zone — that's real, not a fluke — but the power hasn't backed it up: his .168 ISO at the level translates to just a .135 mark in MLB-equivalent terms, below the average big-league hitter. The walk rate travels, the thump may not. ValuCast projects him as a bench or platoon bat, with the projection noting more upside than his current production reflects, but this is a prior-season sample and he's cooled slightly in ValuCast's rankings over the last three days.

805796_hitter.text: Arjun Nimmala is a 20-year-old shortstop whose current-season profile at AA shows a contact-first bat with minimal thump—.308 AVG on just .061 ISO over 72 PA, posting an .744 OPS despite a 22.2% strikeout rate. His best work came at A+ (105 PA), where he hit .241 with .483 SLG and a 15.2% BB rate, signaling more power potential than what's shown recently, but the A+ line still projects to just .134 ISO in MLB translation. The main risk is that power has evaporated in his current AA stint, and at 20 with limited reps, it's unclear whether that's adjustment noise or a real loss of bat strength. He was placed on the injured list in late May, so confidence in this read is limited by both injury status and a thin 72-PA current sample.

805805_hitter.text: Walker Jenkins is a 21-year-old left-handed hitter who genuinely controls the strike zone — across 153 PA this season at AAA and below, he's posting a 15% K rate and a 14% walk rate that translate to a projected 19.6% K and 10.3% BB against MLB pitching, both better than league average. The bat-to-ball ability is the carrying tool here; the power (.188 ISO, four home runs) is solid but not loud, and his projected .147 ISO at the big-league level lands right at the MLB mean. ValuCast has him rising +15.6 in the last three days in their rankings. The projection sees a bench/platoon outcome as most likely (71%), though the approach grade and hit grade suggest there's real everyday upside if the power takes a step — that's the swing variable.

805808_hitter.text: Kevin McGonigle is a 21-year-old contact-and-walk machine who almost never chases — his 17.5% chase rate ranks in the 99th percentile, and his 14.6% walk rate pairs with a 13.8% strikeout rate to give him one of the cleanest plate discipline profiles in the game at his age. The expected production backs it up: an .370 xwOBA (88th percentile) and .274 xBA (79th percentile) say the bat is real even though his 88.1 mph average exit velocity and 37.8% hard-hit rate show he's winning with contact quality and pitch selection rather than raw thump. The projection calls for a .276/.380/.422 line with 14 home runs, 18 steals, and 701 PA — a volume-and-on-base profile that plays anywhere you put him. The one honest question is whether the soft contact numbers catch up to him against better arms, but right now the discipline is so extreme it's the carrying tool.

805809_pitcher.text: Travis Sykora is a 22-year-old right-hander who has been genuinely unhittable in A+ — 14.3 K/9, 2.4 BB/9, a 1.2 ERA, and a 0.7 WHIP across 29.7 innings, numbers that rank at or near the 99th percentile in his pitcher pool. The catch is right there in the sample: under 30 innings, and the data carries a prior-season flag, so take the surface shine with real caution. The MiLB-equivalent translation does hold up enough to matter — his strikeout and command rates project to above-average MLB levels, not just minor-league noise — but the projection sees a depth arm or bullpen piece two to three years out, not a rotation fixture. He's crept up +5 spots in ValuCast's rankings over the last three days, and with a strikeout profile this loud, the interest is understandable, but the workload is too thin to know whether the stuff plays into a starter's frame.

805810_hitter.text: Blake Mitchell is a 21-year-old catcher operating as a high-variance offensive prospect built on elite plate discipline but crippled by contact issues. His 25.4% walk rate ranks in the 99th percentile, and he's posting a .850 OPS with .218 ISO over 272 PA at A+, but a 34.9% strikeout rate (8th percentile) is eating into that value and keeping his .213 average at the basement. The most immediate risk is that he'll never put the ball in play enough to become a usable bat; if the strikeouts don't improve, the walks alone won't sustain even a bench role. With only 272 plate appearances in a thin A+ sample and his approach still raw, confidence in a clear path is modest, though the power base and walk rate suggest more upside than today's hit tool shows.

805906_pitcher.text: Gage Wood is a swing-and-miss machine who hasn't figured out how to throw strikes consistently enough to start — and that tension is the whole story. Across 52 IP between A and AA this season, he's striking out 13.0 per nine while walking 3.6, and his K-BB% sits 96th percentile among arms in the pitcher pool, which tells you the whiff stuff is real even if the command isn't catching up. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his K/9 at 9.1 against a 3.8 BB/9, both roughly league average at the big-league level — fine for a reliever, probably not enough runway for a rotation. The projection has him as a multi-inning or setup arm, with the floor being depth, and that feels right: the miss is an 80, the command is a 45, and until he narrows that gap, the bullpen is where this resolves.

805953_hitter.text: Anthony Huezo is a 20-year-old left-handed hitter generating genuine power—.298 ISO in the 98th percentile—but strangled by swing-and-miss; his 31.3% strikeout rate ranks in the 18th percentile and will cap his floor hard if it doesn't improve. His .909 OPS on 268 plate appearances is real and translates to solid impact, yet the contact collapse is the legitimate risk: when the strikeouts run that high, the hit tool (.259 AVG, 67th percentile) can't recover the value. ValuCast projects him as organizational depth with upside, arriving in two to three years, but the strikeout problem is the gate he must pass through first.

806010_pitcher.text: Barrett Kent is a young starter with elite early command results but a control leak that requires monitoring—27.3 innings of 1.98 ERA and 7.2 K/9 mask a 5.3 BB/9 rate (36th percentile) that sits well above MLB average when translated. The strikeout rate itself ranks at just the 10th percentile for his peer pool, suggesting modest raw stuff paired with decent present command, but the walk rate is the real concern at 4.5 BB/9 translated. This is a stale, thin starter sample from prior-season A-ball; confidence in any read here is low given the 27-inning workload and lack of recent activity.

806046_pitcher.text: Alex Clemmey is a 20-year-old lefty who can miss bats but can't find the zone — and right now, the second half of that sentence is the whole story. At AA this year, he's walking 6.1 per nine across 72.3 innings, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts that at 5.3 BB/9 against a league average of 3.2 — that's a command profile that sits near the bottom of the prospect pitcher pool. The strikeout rate is real enough (9.5 K/9 in AA, translates to roughly league-average 8.1), but a K-BB% that ranks 24th percentile against peers tells you the misses aren't beating the free passes by nearly enough. ValuCast projects a multi-inning or setup reliever ceiling, with a depth arm as the floor, and he's rising nine spots in the rankings over the last three days — but the path there runs straight through fixing the walk rate, because nothing else moves until that does.

806061_hitter.text: Isaiah Drake is a left-handed hitter showing a pull-heavy, power-first approach that hasn't yet translated into consistent contact or on-base skill at A+ ball. Over 296 PA he's hitting .251 with a .411 SLG but a 26.4% strikeout rate and modest 10.1% walk rate—the swings-and-misses are the primary brake on his overall offensive value. His hit and approach grades both sit at 45-level, reflecting a 53 OPS and modest percentile standing, and even his power (ISO .16, 58th percentile) has not offset the offensive drain. The projection floor is organizational depth with a two-to-three-year timeline; current performance suggests medium risk to that floor given the early-stage strikeout profile.

806064_pitcher.text: Steven Echavarria is a 20-year-old A+ starter who is more arm than weapon right now — the walk rate tells the story. 806068_hitter.text: Colt Emerson is a 20-year-old shortstop with real pop for his age — .214 ISO and .469 SLG at AAA translate to a .160 ISO equivalent against MLB pitching, which sits right at the league average for power and is genuinely encouraging for a kid this young. The projection sees a bench or platoon outcome as the most likely landing spot, with the bat's current shape — power present, contact and patience still raw — driving that read. 806071_hitter.text: Farmelo is a 21-year-old center fielder built around patience and impact — his 16% walk rate at A+ is the real headline, translating to an 11.3% MLB-equivalent BB% against a league average of 8.5%. 806146_hitter.text: George Lombard Jr. is a walk machine at 21, and that's not a small thing — his 16% BB rate at AAA+AA translates to a 12.3% MLB-equivalent walk rate against an 8.5% league average, which is the floor his entire offensive game stands on. The .387 OBP over 287 PA is real, built on patience rather than contact, and the 12 stolen bases suggest he's got enough athletic juice to make that on-base frequency mean something. The power is the honest question: his MLB-equivalent ISO (.148) lands right at league average, which is serviceable but not the kind of bat that forces a lineup to work around him. Projection has him as a bench/platoon profile more likely than not, with a low-end everyday ceiling — the approach grades out loud and clear, but the impact has to grow for that ceiling to matter.

806191_hitter.text: Tai Peete is a high-leverage power bat in early A+ ball who trades contact for explosive slugging — his .256 ISO ranks 95th percentile among hitters with 100+ PA, but a 31.4% strikeout rate undercuts the hit tool and approach. At 20 years old with just 140 plate appearances, the sample is fresh and current, though small enough that his true skill remains unsettled; ValuCast projects him as organizational depth over two to three years, with an 85% likelihood of a bench or platoon role. The main risk is whether he can sustain this power profile while cutting the whiffs—translated to MLB, his strikeout rate edges above league average and his isolated power would shrink considerably.

806198_hitter.text: Cooper Pratt is a 21-year-old shortstop who doesn't beat himself — and at Triple-A, that's not nothing. His 14% strikeout rate in 261 PA translates to an MLB-equivalent 18.2% K%, well below the 22.0% league average, and his 13% walk rate becomes a 10.5% equivalent against a big-league norm of 8.5%; the approach is real, not a MiLB mirage. The problem is that the bat doesn't do enough damage yet — his .145 ISO at the level translates to .131 equivalent, and the power hasn't caught up to the contact quality. The projection sees a bench-or-platoon outcome as the most likely landing spot (68%), with a low-end everyday regular as the ceiling — and ValuCast has him moving up +1.3 in the last three days.

806210_hitter.text: Alfonsin Rosario is a 22-year-old power bat at AA who hits the ball very hard and strikes out a lot — those two things are going to be true of him for a while. His .582 SLG and .314 ISO at Double-A put him in the 97th and 98th percentiles among this pool, and the translated ISO of .199 against an MLB average of .150 says the thump carries over even after the level adjustment. The problem is a 32% K-rate that translates to 30.3% against big-league arms, and a walk rate that's essentially average — there's no discipline safety net here, just bat speed meeting mistakes. The projection sees a bench/platoon outcome as most likely, with the ceiling of a low-end everyday regular driven entirely by whether the power stays loud enough to offset the strikeouts, and ValuCast has him moving up +3.3 in the last three days.

806221_hitter.text: Easton Shelton is a 20-year-old power-first hitter with exceptional bat speed and leverage; his .620 slugging and .341 ISO rank in the 99th percentile despite operating in A-ball. The underlying read is loud: he strikes out at 36.6%, well above the 22% MLB average even after translation to 37.7%, which is the main developmental obstacle and a meaningful drag on offensive floor. His walk rate (12.7%) and contact quality are genuine strengths, but the swing-and-miss is severe enough at this stage that consistency and on-base reliability remain unproven questions. The 268 PA sample is current and clean, but translating elite raw power in A-ball to sustained major-league production requires demonstrable strikeout management.

806224_pitcher.text: Brady Smith is a 21-year-old right-hander who does one thing at an elite level right now: miss bats. His 14.8 K/9 and 28% K-BB% through 51.7 innings at A-ball land at the 98th percentile among pitchers in this pool, which is the kind of number that makes you keep watching regardless of what else is on the sheet. The catch is command — a 4.0 BB/9 translates to a projected 4.2 at the MLB equivalent level, and until he tightens that, the projection lands him as a multi-inning or setup reliever rather than a rotation piece, with an 85% probability of becoming a useful MLB arm somewhere in the next two to three years. ValuCast has him cooling slightly, down 36 spots over the last three days, but the miss stuff is real.

806233_hitter.text: Luke Stevenson is a left-handed catcher with an exceptional approach—drawing walks at a 99th-percentile rate (22.7%)—but his contact and power remain well behind the hit-tool demands of a regular. Over 247 PA at A+, he pairs that elite walk rate with a 27.1% strikeout rate and a .217 AVG/.391 SLG, suggesting a player who can work counts but struggles to convert pitches into barrels. The main risk is that his 50-grade hit and impact tools leave little margin for error; even with plus plate discipline, a catcher without average or power will be roofed as depth. ValuCast projects him as organizational depth with a 5% shot at a regular role over two to three years, more optimistic on his long-term trajectory than his current batting line warrants.

806244_pitcher.text: Josh Tiedemann is a strike-thrower early in his A-ball tenure who pounds the zone at a rate (BB/9: 3.1) that ranks in the 83rd percentile but hasn't yet shown the K stuff to separate himself at higher levels—his 10.4 K/9 minor-league rate translates to 8.1 MLB K/9, below league average. The main risk is control sustainability paired with modest strikeout carry; his 1.46 WHIP and 4.24 ERA on a 23.3-inning sample suggest he's walking enough hitters that command alone won't be a path to success without significant velocity or movement development. The current sample is live and fresh but too small to draw firm conclusions about his long-term profile.

806252_hitter.text: Ralphy Velazquez is a 21-year-old first baseman with genuine thunder in the bat — his .483 SLG and .189 ISO across 313 PA at AAA/AA this season put him in the 81st percentile in both slg and power among minor leaguers, and his .386 OBP shows he's not just swinging for fences. The MLB-equivalent translation brings his ISO to .147 and his walk rate to 9.6% (against an 8.5% league average), which is encouraging, though his strikeout rate translates to 22.7% — right at the edge of acceptable. The projection sees an everyday regular ceiling with the impact skill shape already present, but honest odds put him more likely in a bench or platoon role; for a 1B, the bat has to carry everything, and that translated ISO sitting just below average is the number to watch as he climbs. ValuCast has him moving up 10 spots in the last three days.

806258_pitcher.text: Thomas White is a left-handed starter showing high strikeout intent (12.1 K/9 in minor-league action) but limited command; his 4.3 BB/9 and 1.45 WHIP in 18.7 IP at AAA suggest he's still sorting out consistency at the upper minors. MLB-equivalent translation pegs him at 9.2 K/9 and 4.2 BB/9, a K-BB% of 13.6% that sits right at league average—the strikeout upside is real, but so is the walk problem. The main risk is a starter who hasn't yet shown he can repeat his delivery or command; he's pitched just under 25 innings in this sample and remains very much a work in progress with high variance. This is a thin current sample with low confidence in any near-term read.

806263_hitter.text: Brandon Winokur is a young third baseman whose patient approach (14.6 BB%) at A+ keeps him on base at a respectable rate (.378 OBP), but the strikeout rate (29.6 K%) is outpacing his power output (0.169 ISO), creating a contact-and-command mismatch that limits offensive ceiling. The walk rate ranks 75th percentile among comparable prospects, yet the strikeout profile lands only 26th, signaling a hitter who makes contact decisions better than he executes them. His organizational depth ranking and mixed shape over 280 plate appearances suggest a prospect still calibrating his swing; confidence in this sample is appropriately tempered by the translation gap between A+ performance and major-league equivalent outcomes.

806265_pitcher.text: Blake Wolters is a 21-year-old right-handed pitcher operating with poor command and high volatility at A+, unable to contain contact in a shallow 27-inning sample. The core risk is real: a 12.33 ERA that places him at the 1st percentile signals he is not executing his stuff, and the walk rate suggests mechanical or mental inconsistency that must improve before this profile holds prospect value. Given the abbreviated sample and known volatility at this level, confidence in the read is appropriately guarded.

806293_pitcher.text: Payton Martin is a high-walk right-handed pitcher running a command deficit that overshadows his solid strikeout rate. His AA minor-league line shows 7.2 K/9 paired with a 4.3 BB/9, yielding a K-BB% of 7.5%—well below league average and ranking him in just the 22nd percentile for that differential. The walk rate is the binding constraint; at 4.1 BB/9 in MLB equivalent, he sits above the 3.2 big-league average and will need material improvement to stick as a starter. The current 58.7-inning sample is fresh and ongoing, but it's still early in the season to forecast sustained change.

806413_pitcher.text: Daniel Guerra is a strikeout machine with a walk problem — 12.2 K/9 and a 3.20 ERA over 54 innings at A+ this year, but 4.2 BB/9 is the number that decides everything. The miss is real — that K/9 translates to 8.8 at the MLB level against an 8.6 average, so the swing-and-miss isn't a level mirage — but the BB/9 moves to 4.1 against a 3.2 league norm, and that gap is where his starter dream quietly closes. ValuCast projects him as a multi-inning or setup arm within two to three years, with a depth-arm floor if the command never tightens, and he's ticked up +0.4 in the last three days in ValuCast's rankings. The bet here is simple: if the walks come down even a turn, the stuff plays late in games; if they don't, he's organizational depth with a good night every few outings.

806884_hitter.text: Luis Escudero is a 20-year-old second baseman showing early power and patience in a small A-ball sample, posting .292/.470/.625 with an ISO of .333 and BB% of 25.8%. With only 66 plate appearances, this read carries low confidence; he needs sustained repetition at higher levels to validate whether the elite walk rate and power are real or a small-sample mirage.
